strengths: The paper is well motivated and clearly written: it identifies two genuine limitations of current VLA driving models (distributional brittleness of behavior cloning and sparse supervision) and proposes a single mechanism (dense world modeling) that addresses both, used as auxiliary supervision and as an intrinsic reward.

The core idea of using world-model image prediction uncertainty (token entropy) as a novelty signal, gated by a PDMS safety threshold, is a clean and sensible design, and the safety-gating addresses the obvious failure mode of rewarding unsafe OOD trajectories.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art PDMS (93.7 with best-of-N) and EPDMS (88.8) on NAVSIM with only a single front-view camera, improving over DriveVLA-W0 on NAVSIM v2 by a clear 2.7 points; additional nuScenes results support generalizability.

Ablations are targeted and informative: dense supervision (Tab. 3) shows complementary gains from RGB and depth generation, and reward-component ablation (Tab. 4) isolates contributions of PDMS reward, image reward, and their combination; qualitative results show concrete safety-critical failure correction after RL.

Good qualitative analysis of the intrinsic reward (Fig. 3), including a case where the image-based bonus captures novelty that L2 error to the ground truth fails to measure; supplementary material provides substantial implementation detail, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim (world-model-uncertainty exploration) is only weakly supported by the evidence: in Tab. 4 the image reward improves PDMS from 90.19 to 90.36 (+0.17), while the bulk of the gain comes from the standard PDMS reward via GRPO. The headline SOTA is thus attributable mostly to GRPO + dense supervision rather than the novel exploration mechanism, and no variance/seeds are reported for this small gain.

The exploration claim is not validated against its stated motivation: the paper argues exploration helps OOD generalization, but all evaluation is on the in-distribution NAVSIM navtest split; no held-out/OOD scenario experiments are provided to show the policy actually generalizes better due to exploration.

Token-level entropy of a MAGVIT-v2 quantizer is a crude uncertainty proxy; it may conflate visual complexity or perceptual difficulty with trajectory novelty, and no calibration analysis, sensitivity study of the bonus function f(.), the threshold delta, or the weight lambda is provided.

Fig. 3 (left) shows the exploration bonus is positively correlated with L2 error to the expert trajectory, which suggests the bonus rewards deviation from expert behavior; the counterexample in the right panel is a single anecdote, and the tension with safety is not fully resolved.
The 'geometric supervision' from depth is weaker than claimed because ground-truth depth is pseudo-labels from a monocular model (Metric3D); no discussion of how depth-label noise affects results.

The proposed dense-supervision component has limited novelty on its own: jointly training VLA driving models with future image generation is well explored (DriveVLA-W0, UniDrive-WM, PWM, FutureSightDrive, DrivingGPT), so the incremental contribution relative to this line should be stated more carefully.

The nuScenes generalizability results are mixed: L2 error trails OpenDriveVLA and AutoVLA, and UniAD-protocol collision rates are not reported; nuScenes also omits the RL stage, so the core contribution is untested there.

Some methodological details are underspecified: how the world model is conditioned on candidate trajectories during GRPO rollout scoring, how the trajectory-conditioned future generation is performed autoregressively, and the computational cost of generating F future frames per candidate (a significant practical concern with G=8 rollouts).

strengths: Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art PDMS (93.7) and EPDMS (88.8) on NAVSIM using only a single front-view camera, outperforming multi-sensor baselines (DriveSuprim, Centaur), which is a notable efficiency result.

The two-stage framework is coherently designed: the same world model serves both as a dense supervisory signal during imitation learning and as a source of intrinsic reward during RL post-training, and the safety gate (PDMS > δ) on the exploration bonus is a sensible safeguard.

Ablations cover both main components (Tables 3 and 4), separately quantifying the effect of RGB/depth generation and of each reward term, and the qualitative analysis (Figs. 3, 4) attempts to probe the reward design rather than only reporting aggregates.
Related work coverage is thorough and the paper positions itself reasonably well against recent unified understanding-and-generation driving models (DriveVLA-W0, UniDrive-WM, PWM, FSDrive).
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is incremental. Both ingredients exist in prior work: dense world-modeling supervision for driving VLAs (DriveVLA-W0, UniDrive-WM, FSDrive, PWM) and uncertainty-based intrinsic exploration rewards are standard RL tools. The contribution is largely a combination plus GRPO/LoRA post-training on top of an off-the-shelf backbone (Show-o, MAGVIT-v2, Phi-1.5).

The headline exploration mechanism has very weak measured impact: in Table 4, the image-based exploration reward adds only +0.17 PDMS over the PDMS-reward-only baseline (90.19 → 90.36). The paper's central claimed contribution thus accounts for a marginal fraction of the improvement, and no variance or repeated-run statistics are reported to support even this small delta.

The SOTA claim rests heavily on the best-of-N (N=6) selection strategy borrowed from [58]: without it, PDMS is 90.4, behind DriveSuprim (93.5) and DriveVLA-W0† (93.0). The framing of Table 1 does not clearly separate what comes from the method versus the selection strategy.

Fig. 3 is internally contradictory and undercuts the paper's own argument. The introduction argues that uncertainty reflects distance to the *entire* training distribution and is 'more reliable than trajectory distance alone', yet Fig. 3 (left) shows the exploration bonus is positively correlated with L2 error to the single ground-truth trajectory. No quantitative analysis validates the 'distributional novelty' claim, and the core assumption that mask-token prediction entropy measures trajectory-level OOD-ness (rather than inherent stochasticity of future visual content) is never tested.

nuScenes evaluation is weak and one-sided: only Stage 1 is evaluated (no RL), L2 error (0.44m avg ST-P3; 0.77m UniAD) is worse than several baselines (OpenDriveVLA 0.33m, AutoVLA 0.70m), and the best 'collision rate' result comes with missing entries under the UniAD protocol. This does not substantiate the generalizability claim.

Key technical details are under-specified or unexamined: the bounding function f(·) in Eq. (6) is never defined; the sensitivity to the exploration weight λ and threshold δ is not studied; there is no discussion of reward hacking (e.g., the policy gaming entropy or EP metrics); and the large EC gap versus DriveVLA-W0 (86.8 vs 58.9) that contributes substantially to the EPDMS margin is not explained.

Writing quality issues remain (e.g., 'patial layout' on p.8), Eq. (1) is trivial, and no code or anonymized link is provided despite the reproducibility promise, which is important given the many interacting components (tokenizers, backbone, GRPO configuration, reward shaping).

strengths: Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art PDMS (93.7) and EPDMS (88.8) on NAVSIM using only a single front-view camera, outperforming multi-sensor methods, with additional validation on nuScenes.

The dual use of the world model — as dense auxiliary supervision (future RGB + depth token prediction) and as a source of intrinsic novelty reward via prediction entropy — is an elegant and coherent framing that connects the two stated limitations of VLA driving models (sparse supervision, lack of exploration).

Well-designed ablations: Table 3 cleanly isolates the contribution of RGB vs. depth generation (86.2 -> 88.5 PDMS), and Table 4 isolates each reward component during GRPO post-training, giving reasonable visibility into which parts of the system matter.
The qualitative analysis of the exploration bonus (Fig. 3) and the safety-critical failure cases corrected by RL post-training (Fig. 4) provide useful intuition beyond aggregate metrics.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-motivated problem formulation, complete equations for the losses and rewards, and implementation details (hyperparameters, hardware, thresholds) sufficient for approximate reproduction.
weaknesses: The headline conceptual contribution — the uncertainty-based exploration bonus — is only weakly supported by the evidence: Table 4 shows the image reward alone improves PDMS by only 0.03 (88.50 -> 88.53), and combined with the PDMS reward it adds just 0.17 over PDMS-reward-only (90.19 -> 90.36). The bulk of the gain comes from GRPO with a PDMS reward, which prior work (e.g., AutoVLA, RecogDrive) already establishes. The paper's most novel claim thus rests on a marginal quantitative margin with no variance/significance analysis.

There is a tension in the novelty analysis: Fig. 3 (left) reports a 'generally positive correlation' between the exploration bonus and L2 error to the ground-truth trajectory, which undercuts the paper's argument that prediction entropy is a better novelty signal than trajectory deviation; only a single anecdotal counterexample (Fig. 3, right) supports the claimed advantage. A systematic evaluation of the entropy-based novelty measure against alternatives (e.g., ensembles, RND-style predictors, feature-space distances) is missing.

The framing contains an inconsistency: the introduction argues that autonomous driving 'enjoys neither advantage' of simulators and that 'no existing simulator faithfully captures' scene dynamics, yet the reward in Eq. (7) relies on PDMS, which is computed via NAVSIM's pseudo-simulation. The world model is never actually used to provide state transitions during RL, so the 'learned world model to anticipate action consequences' motivation is only partially realized in the method.

Token-level entropy over the MAGVIT-v2 codebook is a crude uncertainty proxy; it conflates aleatoric ambiguity (e.g., multimodal futures, inherently uncertain appearance) with epistemic OOD-ness, and the paper provides no analysis of failure modes where high entropy corresponds to simply visually ambiguous-but-safe futures. The bounding function f(.) and entropy normalization are also underspecified in the main text.

The best-of-N (N=6) results marked with † complicate the SOTA claim, since selection among sampled candidates is itself a strong inference-time strategy; the paper should more clearly separate the contribution of training from that of test-time sampling (this matters because the world-model exploration is claimed to improve the policy itself).

nuScenes results are mixed and partially incomplete: L2 errors are worse than EMMA and OpenDriveVLA under both protocols, and UniAD-protocol collision rates are absent for the proposed model, weakening the cross-benchmark generalization claim.

Conceptual novelty is moderate: uncertainty/prediction-error-based intrinsic rewards are well studied in RL, and combining world models with RL post-training for driving is explored in closely related concurrent work (World4Drive, PWM, DriveVLA-W0, AD-R1); the paper's differentiation from these is largely at the level of the specific reward construction rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.
